Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Ashraf al-Ḥusaynī al-Samarqandī was a 13th century Islamic theologian, astronomer and mathematician from Samarkand, now in Uzbekistan. Born in the 1220s, al-Samarqandī was a prominent figure in the Islamic Golden Age, contributing significantly to the fields of theology, astronomy, and mathematics. His most notable work, the “Sharh al-Mawaqif’, is still studied today for its insights into the principles of astronomy and cosmology.

His contributions were heavily influenced by the works of Avicenna and Averroes, and he built upon their ideas to develop his own unique theories. Al-Samarqandī's work had a profound impact on the development of Islamic theology and the understanding of the natural world, making him one of the most important figures in the history of Islamic scholarship.

The legacy of al-Samarqandī can be seen in the many institutions and schools of thought he influenced, including the famous Madrasa al-Samarqandī in Samarkand, which became a hub for Islamic learning and intellectual inquiry. His writings also inspired later scholars, such as Ibn Khaldun, who built upon his ideas to develop his own theories of history and society.

In the end, al-Samarqandī's contributions to the world of Islamic scholarship and learning left a lasting impact that can still be felt today, making him a figure of great historical significance.

Shams al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Ashraf al-Ḥusaynī al-Samarqandī was a polymath who made significant contributions to theology, astronomy, and mathematics during the 13th century Islamic Golden Age.
